column2: As Olson took more and more command of the college, its patriarchal hierarchy grew stronger, replicating the outside order despite a little more room for maneuver. Consequences: Natasha's ouster; the exclusion of the alternative she represented.

Years later, Betty died in a head-on collision with an oncoming car at dusk one winter. Rumaker wonders whether she did not throw herself into it deliberately, having lost herself in Charles's shadow. Winter dusk, head-on collision

Olson recommended to his students Sappho, Gertrude Stein's “Melanctha” (the only work of fiction by a woman he thought worthwhile), Jane Harrison's Prolegomena, and Ruth Benedict's Patterns of Culture, which circulated from hand to hand thanks to him; he called these women, in a tone of amusement and wonder, “vestal virgins.” Patterns of Culture in paperback

With almost no money left for coal (reserved for the Studies Building alone), the students form crews with Olson, felling trees with a new portable chainsaw that makes everyone, Charles included, a little nervous; deadfall and trees are sawed into logs to feed the stoves in the houses. Frequent breaks for man talk: there is discreet discussion of Karen Karnes's voluptuous body, displayed that summer in the Tableaux and ranked in the pantheon of female fantasies alongside Marilyn Monroe in Niagara; Terence Burns claims to hear her sighing heavily at night through the wall of his study from the room she shared with David, and dreams of going to console her. A new chainsaw; a circular saw

The coal supply keeps dwindling in the huge outdoor hopper of the Studies Building; on very cold nights, with not enough coal in the lodges, several students sleep in their studies. After the move up to the cottages from the south campus, Tom, Terence, and Rumaker take turns at the Meadows Inn furnace, in a tiny, claustrophobic dirt cellar under Tom's room: it takes a lot of wood to heat the boiler and push the steam to the radiators; Rumaker fears the antique will explode. The big lobby fireplace is used too. Merely tending the furnace is enough to warm up and forget the bitter mountain cold.

One night, while Dan, Cynthia, Jorge, and David are drinking beer in the lobby, Merrill draws Rumaker to him and lies face down; Rumaker enters him, then pulls out to prolong it; Merrill shrieks with rage that he has ruined everything and does not know how to do it, crying that Herb would know how; the lobby falls silent, and Cynthia giggles. Saliva as lubricant, dubbed Black Mountain Vaseline; thin pine walls; stifled laughter Consequences: The couple's real breakup; Jorge gives a knowing smile the next day; the others show nothing

After long weeks of abstinence, Merrill draws Rumaker to him and turns over on his stomach without foreplay; Rumaker spits into his hand, enters him, pulls out to hold back and prolong it; Merrill writhes, shrieking that he has ruined everything and that only Herb would know how; silence in the lobby, Cynthia's giggle; the next day, Jorge's knowing smile, the others' indifference Words: Merrill: “What the hell are you doing? Why'd you do that, you fool!” Atmosphere: The murmur of conversation on the other side of the thin wall, blood pounding in his ears, shame at being overheard Stakes: The end of the couple, consummated publicly in spite of themselves; Rumaker keeps quiet like a sheepish altar boy

One Saturday night, one of the last parties before the lower campus closes completely. Merrill asks Rumaker whether he is going; Rumaker, barely speaking, lies that he has work to do, out of pride and to punish him. Merrill has had a bottle of wine bought in Asheville and offers to share it; Rumaker refuses. After his supper dishwashing shift, he watches Merrill bathe, dress, and leave without a word. Wine bought in Asheville, as against the gasoline-tasting moonshine punch cut with iced tea and Bert Morgan's 25-cent home brew with its yeast to let settle; a dressy red polo shirt sent by Merrill's mother from Kewanee; clean jeans; the bottle in its brown paper bag Consequences: The last image: Rumaker left alone, hurt, wanting to hold him back

Thanksgiving Day in the United States: after a visit to the building site (“wunderbar”), he has lunch with his hosts and they talk at length about the present state of Germany. He judges Inge Aicher-Scholl truly the most intelligent and kindest of them all.

Reflecting no doubt on the first Thanksgiving weekend of 1933, which coincided with their arrival in New York, he writes to Anni that they should give thanks together for all they have accomplished, seen, and created over the past years.
The first weekend, the Aichers take him by car to the nearby Alpine towns; the Baroque architecture of the South delights him and strengthens his first sensory impression before Ulm Cathedral.

The following week he visits Ludwig and Maude Grote, friends from the Dessau days; together they go to Bamberg, an incredibly large and old town, all preserved and wonderful; he writes that he walks all day in the shadow of cathedrals and feels it as a blessing.

Merrill's curt question, “Are you going tonight?”; Rumaker's lie (“I've got work to do”); the offer of wine refused; after the evening dishes, back to Streamside; the sound of the bath draining; images of Merrill's body; drawers opening; a mad hope that he will come back and plead; Merrill walks through without a word, in the red polo shirt from his mother in Kewanee, clean jeans, the bottle in a brown bag, his cheeks the color of the wild roses at the Gatehouse Words: Merrill: “Are you going tonight?”; Rumaker: “I've got work to do.” Atmosphere: Water draining noisily, Rumaker's breath cut short, desire and wounded pride Stakes: The last missed chance at reconciliation; Rumaker punishes himself by punishing Merrill with his absence

Josef accepts an invitation and returns to Germany for the first time since the war, to teach for two months at Ulm A stay of exactly two months Consequences: His first return to Germany since the war

After accusing the college of nonpayment and then apologizing (his lawyers had entered the payments in another account), Forbes agrees to defer a $1,000 note that is due. $1,000 deferred; an accounting error by Forbes's lawyers

Rumaker rents a cramped, stuffy room in a boardinghouse, drawn by the price and the sounds of the river; he stays a month or two, working at Prentice-Hall. $4 a week; clean sheets handed out once a week; rent expected on time; his trunk shipped by rail freight from the college; $2 wasted on a taxi for a few blocks
Several old friends receive him and fete him; he relishes the paintings of Dürer, Altdorfer, and their contemporaries in the museums.
A short Christmas holiday spent in Bottrop and the surrounding area, including his beloved Sauerland; back in Ulm for the new year.

Shortly before Christmas, Albers receives by airmail a small silver-lined wooden box containing 24 white envelopes the size of calling cards, each a miniature color study by a painting student; he writes to Anni that he was moved by it. A silver-lined wooden box, 24 white envelopes, sent by airmail Consequences: Albers wonders what to give in return

Crossing letters: Anni passes on that Charly and others want Albers back for the next term; Sawyer details two problems: the Advanced Painting students find the visiting critic Burgoyne Diller somewhat limited, and the sculpture program lacks coherence and leadership. Letters crossing on the same day Consequences: Albers insists to Sawyer that sculpture will not succeed without funding
Cage's statement “No subject/No image…” on Rauschenberg's White Paintings appears in Emily Genauer's column in the New York Herald Tribune The phrase “No subject/No image …”

A visit to the stuffy room; the landlady drags out the price and the rules; Rumaker accepts, drawn by the price and the boats' horns; he lives there alone among invisible lodgers, reading in his corner armchair; a mute encounter on the dark stairs with a made-up, drunken woman who smiles at him shyly. Words: The landlady: four dollars a week, clean sheets handed out once a week, rent expected on time. Atmosphere: Stuffy, silent, foghorns in the distance, face powder and lipstick on the stairs Stakes: The solitude and poverty of the apprentice writer away from the college

Shortly before Christmas, a small silver-lined wooden box arrives by airmail: 24 white envelopes the size of calling cards, each a miniature color study by a painting student; Albers writes to Anni of his emotion and his embarrassment: what to give in return? Words: “Today a beautiful small wooden box (silver-lined)... It really made me feel quite emotional. What can I do in return?” Atmosphere: A distant holiday, tenderness, and nostalgia for Yale Stakes: The living bond between Albers and his students despite the ocean

Elaine has her first solo show only in 1954, six years after her first review in ARTnews; she admits that being known as an art critic may have delayed her recognition as a painter. A 6-year gap between the first review and the first solo show
The young artist finds the affair unsettling because of the other women who come and go and the sharp increase in Bill's drinking since 1953.

A dilapidated eight-room Victorian house named for the color of its paint; Kline, with his companion Nancy Ward, and Ludwig Sander join them; Bill paints in the garage; a wildly social season: Rosenberg and the dealers Kootz, Castelli, and Janis in the Hamptons; Joan Mitchell and Mimi and Paul Brach rent a house on Fireplace Road (The Springs), where the Zogbaums and the Pollocks also live. Consequences: Elaine: a pleasant but nightmarish summer, with too many friends, too much conversation, too much drinking, too much of a good thing

A very social summer, which Elaine called pleasant but nightmarish, with too many friends, conversations, and drinks. Joan Mitchell and the Brachs rent a house on Fireplace Road; the Zogbaums and the Pollocks live there too; art dealers (Kootz, Castelli, Janis) live in the Hamptons

The start of the annual softball game in the Zogbaums' yard. For one game, Elaine, Bill, and Kline painted a coconut and two grapefruits to look like balls; Rosenberg pitched them to the sculptor Philip Pavia, who swung with full force, to general laughter. Wilfrid Zogbaum could not play: having tossed a lit match into the stove of his shack, he had caused an explosion that gave him third-degree burns. A painted coconut and two painted grapefruits; third-degree burns Consequences: An important annual event for Elaine; a few years later she writes to Pavia, joking about upstarts who have taken over their baseball game.

Cornelia, 77, had not seen her son for nearly twenty years. Bill sold several paintings to pay for her crossing. Marjorie drove them to the ship in Hoboken; Cornelia talked nonstop, in Dutch. At the Red House she talks to everyone despite the language barrier; in the evening, mother and son stroll peacefully along Main Street like Dutch burghers. Obsessed with cleanliness (she gets up early to scrub the steps and tells at length over dinner, translated by Bill, how she used to clean the garbage can), she hates Bill's current paintings and criticizes his drinking and his erratic marriage. 77 years old; nearly 20 years without seeing her son; several paintings sold for the crossing
A wall hanging made in 1954, based on a pre-Columbian Peruvian motif resembling a Greek key, the future basis of the Meander screenprints. Consequences: The motif taken up again in Meander (1970)

With Connie gone to Scituate (Massachusetts) with Kate, Robert brings Olson to dinner every evening; that summer, Olson becomes involved with Betty Kaiser; he wears a fresh white shirt every evening and enjoys Helen's French dinners. A new white shirt every evening; French cooking Consequences: Helen reads Call Me Ishmael as soon as she can and discovers William Carlos Williams's In the American Grain thanks to Olson

At the end of the summer of 1954, Stefan Wolpe finishes an opera after Ibsen's Peer Gynt, performed by almost the whole college as both cast and audience: Hellman sings Peer Gynt, Olson plays the Great Boyg and the Button Molder. Roles: Hellman as Peer Gynt, Olson as the Boyg and the Buttonmaker; Stefan at the piano, regretfully stretching out the rehearsals

Huss directs a very moving staged reading of Uncle Vanya (Hellman as Vanya, Helen as Sonya, Betty as the young wife), at which Stefan Wolpe sheds tears, then scenes from Ghosts in which Helen plays Mrs. Alving and Michael Rumaker her son. Weeks of rehearsal for a few moments of acting Consequences: Through the coaching, Helen discovers the transformation of voice and body

Low printing costs in Majorca: the Creeleys carry on alone, rename the business Divers Press, and publish, among others, Mayan Letters (about a quarter of the letters Olson wrote from Yucatán), Olson's In Cold Hell, in Thicket, Blackburn's Proensa and The Dissolving Fabric, Layton's In the Midst of My Fever, Eigner's From the Sustaining Air, and Duncan's Caesar's Gate. Consequences: This core will feed The Black Mountain Review.

Rexroth, who had joined the board rather casually, withdraws after the first issue: two articles by Seymour-Smith criticizing the adoration of Theodore Roethke and Dylan Thomas seem too harsh to him. Creeley answers in a note in the fall 1954 issue, reaffirming the value of the attack on Roethke's diffuseness and generality. Consequences: An illustration of the magazine's polemical tone.

Published in the spring of 1954, on schedule. It opens with Olson's “On First Looking Out of La Cosa's Eyes”; poems by Creeley, Blackburn, Layton, and Eigner; Creeley's introduction to eight reproductions of paintings by René Laubiès (one of Pound's first French translators); Olson's “Against Wisdom As Such”; the rest in prose, by authors who remained obscure. 64 pages, weighted toward prose. Consequences: Excitement in some circles during the McCarthy years; Blackburn canvasses New York bookstores for distribution.

Duncan's first appearance in the magazine (issue 3, fall 1954). Levertov takes the poem for a parody of her style; Olson thinks it is an attack on him. Lines quoted: “inspired/the aspirate / the aspirant almost / without breath”. Consequences: Duncan's momentary isolation.

Desperate to leave Majorca, Creeley, who had never taught or held a real job, arrives at eight in the morning after driving all night from New York in a 1940 pickup truck. He knocks at Olson's door: a first meeting with a colossal man wrapped in a towel, otherwise naked, who warmly invites him in. After breakfast, Olson draws him in despite himself, and on the very evening of his arrival Creeley is in front of a class. A 1940 Ford pickup; 8 a.m.; a bath towel; his wife had cabled him that if he really could not do it, he should simply come back. Consequences: Creeley becomes a central figure of the college's last years

Six students grouped at one end of an enormous table, Creeley alone at the other end, looking sideways at the wall, dabbing his lost eye with a handkerchief. Having left off his eye patch out of shyness, his injured eye streams under the emotion. He talks without stopping, so low and in such a deep, rasping voice that no one understands. Karen Karnes asks him to speak up; he raises his voice for a few minutes, then falls back into a monotone. An enormous table taking up almost the whole room; a handkerchief; an eye lost in an accident, an eye patch usually worn; six students Consequences: The class then moves to a smaller room, and things improve

After that terrifying first evening, Creeley begins reading aloud the poetry that matters to him (a lot of Hart Crane and William Carlos Williams, rarely his own) and talking about the jazz musicians whose music is essential to him: Miles Davis, Charlie Parker, Bud Powell. Hart Crane, William Carlos Williams, Miles Davis, Charlie Parker, Bud Powell Consequences: Within a few weeks he forms deep attachments, in class and out

During this period, Jonathan Williams publishes at Jargon Press a book of poems by Creeley with drawings by Dan Rice, titled “All That is Lovely in Men.” Poems by Creeley, drawings by Dan Rice, Jargon Press

Creeley, a heavy drinker, is in the habit of walking three or four miles in the afternoon to Ma Peak's tavern to get drunk. On class nights, Grey Stone arrives in a pickup, takes him in tow, brings him back to the college, and tells him: “Now, teach.” 3-4 miles on foot; a pickup; “Now, teach.” Consequences: Creeley eventually eases up on the bottle

The service stops abruptly the day Grey Stone finds in the trash cans scraps of paper on which Creeley had worked on his poems. That Creeley practices a craft, that his poems do not spring fully formed from his head, is unforgivable to Grey Stone. Scraps of paper thrown in the trash cans

The farm had carried on for a while after the communal kitchen closed: vegetables and lettuce were available, and Doyle Jones still raised enough chickens to feed everyone, but few had the stomach to clean them after slaughter; Barbara Leeb remembers vomiting on the entrails when she tried. Doyle resigns in 1954, the cows are sold, the farm dies out, removing the extra source of free food. Hot plates and small refrigerators take over. Freshly killed chickens, entrails; cows sold; hot plates

The community is down to nine students and half a dozen “staff,” but the emphasis on doing one's work has intensified: how else to justify the group's existence except as a refuge for the world's accursed talents? The Black Mountain Review contributes greatly to this (above all to the writers' egos). Wes Huss writes to Paul Williams in the spring of 1954 that, in inverse proportion to the economic setbacks, the quality of the work seems to be rising. 9 students, ~6 staff members; Huss's letter to Paul Williams

Williams, who had personally given $6,500 in 1953 and taken a $25,000 first mortgage on the farm, has all but given up hope of setting Black Mountain right; he sets up his own colony at Stony Point, essentially a housing cooperative based on neighborliness and readily available consolation. $6,500 given in 1953; $25,000 mortgage Consequences: Karen Karnes and David Weinrib join Stony Point in 1955; the colony will later include Cage, Cunningham, Mary Caroline Richards, and David Tudor.

A purely pro forma Advisory Council is announced, with dazzling names; Einstein is persuaded to provide a statement, dated January 16, 1954, of his faith in the importance of BMC. Einstein's statement dated January 16, 1954 Consequences: A publicity stunt with no real financial effect

Rumaker shares an apartment with Mary Ann Fretz during winter vacation; Bert, who left the college the year before for the army, is civil but distant, not very talkative. Consequences: Another Black Mountain episode, over as quickly as it began
After the bad relations between Olson and Doyle had soured ties with the community, Doyle gives up his post as farm manager for good in 1954.

Nearly a year after hearing it, Rumaker grasps Wolpe's paradoxical lesson (helped by Olson's repetitions) and uses it in the first calf story he writes, in Olson's class. Years later, he puts it this way: “The lie of the imagination creates the truth of reality.” A later formulation: “The lie of the imagination creates the truth of reality” Consequences: This idea gives him permission to use his imagination and frees him to write; he remains especially grateful to Wolpe for it.

The lower half of the campus, including the kitchen, the dining hall, and the North and South Lodges, is closed; everyone moves to the small cottages and the barracks-like buildings (“Chances”) beyond the Studies Building. Kitchen and dining hall closed; North and South Lodges closed; everyone has to cook for himself and get supplies from the farm Consequences: A shrinking of space and of basic amenities

Olson, now Rector, and the few remaining teachers try everything: bulletins with exaggerated course announcements, the college's timber cut and leased to local loggers, a trip by Olson to New York to solicit the Ford Foundation. An old Ford convertible (the irony of the make); GI benefits of a few veterans that help keep the college open Consequences: The Ford Foundation, liberal by reputation but stiff in reality, stays deaf even to Olson's flattery; nothing works

Olson, in class, rages against the Asheville Citizen photograph showing “boy scientists” exulting after a nuclear success, like teenagers at a party, oblivious to the consequences. A newspaper photograph; the fallout of “clean” and “dirty” bombs discussed in class

During this period Creeley writes a poem featuring Liz, the college's ancient cat, on the question of whether or not he was making it. Liz, a cat with one pink eye and one green eye, always pregnant despite her great age.

Betty abruptly leaves the college and returns to New York, officially to resume her musical career, in reality to give birth to Charles Olson's child. Betty's apartment on West 72nd Street in New York Consequences: The birth of Olson and Betty's infant son in New York

One late afternoon, Rumaker runs into Olson in town clothes, a dress shirt, a rumpled bow tie, a seersucker jacket, carrying a dark leather suitcase, heading for his convertible. Connie comes out after him, her face tense. Caught by Rumaker, Olson gives up: he turns around, finger to his lips, shushing, and goes back into the house with Connie. Rumaker thinks Olson was perhaps going to join Betty and his son in New York. A dress shirt, a rumpled bow tie, his only seersucker jacket, a battered leather suitcase, a convertible, a gray mustache, a finger pressed to his lips Consequences: Olson stays at the college; Rumaker interprets the scene as an aborted escape

Since Olson has been seeing Betty Kaiser, persistent rumors of marital trouble circulate among the students; Connie's increasingly closed silence and pained eyes lend them credence. Rumaker will later discover that Charles and Connie were not legally married. Olson's furtive nighttime visits upstairs at Meadows Inn Consequences: An atmosphere of unease in the disintegrating community

Almost every night, Rumaker, whose room is downstairs, hears Olson stealthily climbing the stairs to Betty's room upstairs; he recognizes the step of each of the residents without seeing them. Creaking stairs, heavy steps trying to be light, around midnight Consequences: Rumaker experiences the betrayal as that of a father toward his mother
A symbiotic, epistolary relationship between Olson and Frances Boldereff, with occasional meetings in person; Connie knew about it; the affair was revealed only years later.

After years at the college, Fee Dawson's 2-S student status ends and he is drafted for the Korean War; he leaves the college. A worn jean jacket and Levi's Consequences: Rumaker is relieved to see him go

After a few weeks of flirting (the raft on Lake Eden, walks), Fee says to Rumaker on the way down to South Lodge: “You knew it had to come to this”. That evening, he does not show up for the rendezvous in Rumaker's room and does not answer when Rumaker knocks at his door. Rumaker concludes he was making fun of him, like Ellen Schasberger in the spring of 1953. Waiting, sitting on the bed; a bright summer afternoon Consequences: Rumaker avoids Fee afterward; a link with the memory of Ellen Schasberger

One evening, Olson reads in class Douglas Woolf's story “The Kind of Life We've Planned,” a manuscript sent by Creeley from Mallorca. The students collectively scorn it; Olson, furious, rebukes them for their obtuseness and announces that the story will appear in the summer 1954 issue of The Black Mountain Review and must be reread carefully. A story about golfers judged “corny” and melodramatic by the students; Ed Dorn and Jorge Fick the most vehement in their scorn; the plot involves a lie and a false rape. Consequences: Rumaker, rereading it, discovers a “wry-eyed” American writer; Woolf's first novel, Hypocritic Days, will be published by Creeley at Divers Press, and its first chapters, arriving from Spain and read aloud by Olson in class, open up the field of fiction for several students.

To recruit Black students after the legal desegregation of 1954, Olson invites a Black minister from Asheville and his wife, fusses awkwardly over the tea looking for uncracked cups, and praises a school where Black and white would work together, mentioning Jacob Lawrence in 1946 and the few Black students at the summer sessions. All goes well until Kate Olson (2) and then baby David Huss arrive, both naked, Kate dragging a dead bird by the wing. Kate: “The fuckin' owl did it”; the minister: “Oh! What happened to the poor bird?”; Kate's big, grave brown eyes. Consequences: The couple's shocked faces: no student will be recommended to Black Mountain.

Before Fee leaves for the army, Olson gives his current events class, Olson-style, in the morning (unusual for him, who prefers the energies of the night). The central text: the Asheville Citizen, to be read every day. An analysis of John Foster Dulles's hidden motives, of the vocabulary of “clean bombs” versus “dirty bombs,” of the dangers of nuclear fallout. Extra copies of the Citizen stocked at Carroll's; battered old car seats in the Reading Room; Olson takes up the space of several people; he thought as little of Time's style as of McCarthy's pernicious oratory. Consequences: Rumaker writes a paper on Truman's handling of the American steel strike (sources: old issues of Time in the library); Olson, much impressed, says he admires his ability to write a paper in spite of his sources; Rumaker feeds on it for days.

Having refused to go back to the factories (including the shipyard with his father), Rumaker accepts, out of the goodness of Olson's heart as he sees it, to clean for $5 the high slit windows, opaque with chimney and cigarette smoke, and dust hundreds of books on wall shelves. $5; a tall, rickety stepladder; narrow slit windows near the ceiling; hundreds of books Consequences: The money lets him eat for a few more weeks, thanks to Tom's frugal menus and shopping at the A&P in Black Mountain.
Perched on the stepladder, Rumaker mischievously tells the visitor in a suit who has come to see Olson that he is the houseboy; Olson, amused and barely piqued, smiles back at him.

Back from his military service in West Germany, Williams brings extra copies of The Maximus Poems 1-10 printed in Stuttgart; a well-lubricated evening follows, perhaps in celebration. Printed in Stuttgart; bourbon and Ma Peak's beer at the party Consequences: The drunken party leads to the nighttime outing to the lake with Rumaker.

After the party, Williams suggests a nighttime skinny-dip; they drive in his little black Hillman Minx along winding country roads and lie down naked side by side on a sandy beach. Seized by a sudden, sober fear (hill people hidden in the trees watching them, two naked men), Rumaker insists on going back; Williams, exasperated, finally gives in and takes him back to his visitor's room at Streamside. A black Hillman Minx; moonlight, ash-white sand; trees pressing in all around Consequences: Back to Streamside, safe.

Flola Shepard, the language teacher, lets mice live in her quarters, setting out dozens of sardine cans filled with scraps on the floors and shelves. When she leaves in 1954, Hellman, the newly appointed writer, moves in; Rumaker, paid a few dollars, helps prepare the lodgings and clean up countless mouse droppings; Hellman also insists that he scrub the toilet bowl, fearing a brown line on his buttocks. Dozens of sardine cans; hundreds of rodents according to Rumaker; a few dollars earned Consequences: Hellman not an easy employer; Rumaker feels he really earned the money.

One Sunday evening, Hellman reads his work; Olson warns him firmly: “Stop trying to be Tolstoy”. Hellman also reads a curious story from his wartime days in Australia: a voyeur hidden in the bushes watching naked soldiers bathe, told with the homophobic overtones of the period but fascinating to Rumaker for its homoerotic implications. Consequences: Despite this, Olson pushes Hellman to teach writing, Creeley being in Mallorca.

Rumaker signs up mainly to give Hellman a few students, at Olson's request; Hellman cavalierly disparages everything he writes and loses the only copy of a story by Rumaker about the summer at the shipyard with his father; his rough Bronx manner and his arrogance weigh down the class. The only copy of a story lost Consequences: Rumaker is relieved when the class ends; he misses Creeley's class; he feels it is time to leave, around 1955.

Baker, sitting in on Olson's class, accuses him of deceiving the students by making them believe they are great; Olson replies that the aim of the class, and of the college, is to create Dostoevskys; when she confidently maintains her accusation, he shouts in a voice hoarse with rage: “I'm tough, don't mess with me—I'm dynamite!” Rumaker, on his cane chair, squirms with embarrassment, torn between his loyalty to Olson and his affection for Betty. A cane chair with a creaking slatted back Consequences: Rumaker feels torn once again.

Shortly after the quarrel, in front of the entrance, Olson sneers on seeing her car: what can you expect from someone who drives a Plymouth, and a Cranbrook model at that! A car parked in front of the Studies Building Consequences: Rumaker concludes: no wonder she packs up in December.

In Wes's theater class, Rumaker plays Chris, the grumpy old captain in Anna Christie, while the new student Lorraine (from New York, future wife of Harvey Harmon in San Francisco in 1957) plays Anna, a role Rumaker should have had, identifying as he did with that humiliated queer woman dependent on alcohol. They also give scenes from Molière one Sunday evening: thanks to Wes's patience, Rumaker discovers rhythm, the right pauses, and the joy of being entirely in a role; Wes tells him so, and Olson, without a word, gives the two actors a satisfied wink. Consequences: A first real understanding of Molière and of the pleasure of acting.

One cool fall evening, when a group wants to go to the Roxy movie theater in Swannanoa, Olson imposes an emergency night crew to replace the broken windows of the Studies Building in order to save coal. A few go to the movies anyway; others stay, grumbling, including Rumaker, guilty and loyal. Olson, agitated by the desertions (perhaps a mutiny in the eyes of the former sailor), cuts his thumb deeply on a pane in the lower stairwell, crying “Look at that!”; Rumaker immediately thinks of the line from Marlowe that Olson had quoted in class: “See, see, where Christ's blood streams in the firmament!” Once Olson has gone off to have Connie bandage him, they all scramble into Tom's Buick and catch the first show at the Roxy. Broken windows; saving coal before winter; Tom's Buick; the show at the Roxy in Swannanoa Consequences: General defection as soon as the leader is gone.
A discussion of Hart Crane took place one evening in Olson's class; Rumaker thinks it was probably sparked by Creeley's poem “Hart Crane (2),” published in Origin II.

Joe Fiore mounts Caresse Crosby's loan exhibition on the lower floor of the Studies Building: Hart Crane's typed letters signed “Hart” in heavy ink, plus books. Rumaker stands in awe before these few originals, disappointed that they are typed, looking in vain for an open mention of homosexuality in the poems. Typed letters, the signature “Hart” in ink; “He had a kind and northern face”. Consequences: Rumaker sees in it an artifact of closeness to a writer near to his own identity.

At Olson's suggestion, to generate publicity and attract students, Mary Fiore writes an announcement of the exhibition; she drives Rumaker in the Jeep station wagon to the office of the Asheville Citizen to have it published. People come from all over the state, surprised that such a small college lost in the western hills should show such pieces, and surprised that the place, run-down as it is, does not look like a real college. Jeep station wagon; the Asheville Citizen. Consequences: Olson's hope of attracting new students fails.

After the exhibition, weeks of indecision and palaver (nothing was ever simple at BMC) over who would return the archives; Olson finally delegates Joe Fiore. Fiore, nervous at having this treasure in the school's keeping (fear of fire, with the 1952 forest fire and the destruction of Roadside still on everyone's mind, and of flooding in rainy weather), puts it all back in the sturdy original trunk and ships it, heavily insured, to Caresse in Washington. The sturdy original trunk, a heavily insured shipment; the memory of the 1952 forest fire.

Wieners hears Olson on the radio in Boston announcing a reading at the Charles Street Meeting House; he goes during Hurricane Hazel and is immediately won over, as Rumaker had been on hearing Ben Shahn talk about Olson in Philadelphia. Hurricane Hazel; Olson despised the radio, “that disembodied voice” Consequences: Wieners decides to go down to Black Mountain

Pollock often arrives drunk in his battered car, takes a beer from the refrigerator, looks for Bill, and offers to wrestle; sober, he goes up to watch old movies (westerns, musicals) with Bill on television. A battered car, a beer from the refrigerator, an old television set, westerns and musicals Consequences: No one agrees to wrestle with Pollock, known as a violent drunk.

Bill's work is selected to represent the United States at the 1954 Venice Biennale; a retrospective at MoMA chosen by Andrew C. Ritchie; inclusion in “the New Decade: 35 American Painters and Sculptors” at the Whitney. 1954 Venice Biennale; Andrew C. Ritchie curator

Charlotte and Jim Brooks, seeing cars parked along the street, stop and join the budding party. Elaine has made hundreds of crepe paper flowers fastened to the trees, then climbed into the trees to perfume them with spray cologne. Bill has painted the seats of the outhouses and laid out the croquet lawn. The guests read the painted seats as an irreverent gesture, an insiders' joke, not in terms of money. Wheelbarrows of hard-boiled eggs, abundant food, hundreds of crepe paper flowers, a spray bottle of cologne, croquet on the lawn, painted outhouse seats Consequences: The seats later become objects of speculation: authentic works by de Kooning or a mere relic of a party?

A film being shot about him; a report on his work to submit in Stuttgart; a last Sunday morning drive with the Aichers to Schwäbisch Gmünd to see the Romanesque church again; a lecture the previous Monday, an enormous success (so they say, as never before); in Munich, more than a hundred listeners at the National Museum, an exceptionally lively session. More than 100 listeners in Munich; the Romanesque church in Schwäbisch Gmünd.
After a series of farewell parties, his students escort him to the station to the sound of a trumpet fanfare. A trumpet fanfare at the station.

Preparing for the annual meeting of the University Council committee, Sawyer reminds Albers of his retirement, due in 1956, and asks him for suggestions for a successor and for future directions. Annual meeting of the University Council Committee on Architecture, Painting, and Sculpture

Absent (visiting the Minneapolis School of Art on the day of the committee's visit), Albers replies with a letter circulated to the members: faith in basic studies (4th-year and Master's students take the 1st-year courses on their own initiative), a plea for a new sculpture in metal, a demand for a full-time teacher who is constitutionally a sculptor, a complaint about the budget, and a successor who must be a successful teacher first, one who considers the students his material. A visit to the Minneapolis School of Art on the day of the meeting

The committee proposes officially abolishing the Department of Design when Albers retires two years later, negotiating terminal financial settlements with unemployable teachers, and then creating a professional training program in design; Sawyer sees it as a roundabout way of dismissing outdated teachers; the memorandum also notes the dean's inability to coordinate the departments. “for consideration by the Provost and the successor committee” Consequences: No recommendation seriously followed; possibly a harbinger of the end of Sawyer's deanship
Howe completes his three-year contract and Schweikher takes over as chairman in early 1954; Sawyer knows him to have very fixed ideas, rather inflexible and Spartan.

Schweikher, backed by Gene Nalle, extends his method of teaching Structures to the 3rd year in 1954; concerted, vocal opposition from colleagues, alumni, and students; the community splits without Howe's political glue, and Howe is recalled in November 1954 to assess the crisis. Howe's return in November 1954 Consequences: Schweikher's leadership is called into question; the rest of the text is cut off

Schweikher, continuing George Howe's work, extends Nalle's method of teaching Structures to the third-year program, provoking immediate, vocal opposition to one man's influence on the school. Consequences: An open crisis; Howe recalled from Yale in November 1954 to assess the crisis

The National Architecture Accrediting Board, visiting Yale that year, takes the political temperature of the crisis and suspends the department's accreditation. Consequences: The controversy smolders all through the spring of 1955, mixing dissension and intrigue
The figurative sculptor Kreis, visiting critic in the second term of 1953-54, has the students carve reliefs in slate.

Around 1954, the college has almost run out of money: the dining hall is closed, there is no more coal to heat the buildings, and the last teachers and students, withdrawn into small cabins on the hill, are, according to some accounts, painfully hungry. Dining hall closed, no coal, hunger in the hillside cabins Consequences: The context of Olson's diagram for saving the college by atomizing it into satellite institutions.

Olson types on onionskin paper a diagram of concentric circles centered on “The College,” branching into quadrants by type of institution (theater, academy, magazine, publishing house) spread across Cambridge, New York, Berkeley, Philadelphia, and San Francisco. North Carolina is at the center with the label “mytho-, archaeo-, bio-, geo-”. It is the dream of a cosmopolitan college of satellite institutions held together by centripetal force. Ink on paper, 8½ × 11 inches; mention of the presses Black Mt Press, Divers Press, Jargon Press, magazines, and the Black Mountain Review (editor R. [Creeley]); an advisory council including C. G. Jung (Zurich), Carl O. Sauer (Berkeley), Norbert Wiener (Cambridge), William Carlos Williams (N.J.), Franz Kline (New York); rector Olson, secretary Joseph [Burden?], treasurer Wesley Huss; fellows including Stefan Wolpe and Anthony Landreau Consequences: The college will nonetheless close in 1957; the diagram embodies the wish for preservation through atomization.

Olson takes over the leadership of the college after Albers, serving as de facto rector before his official appointment in 1954, while the ship sinks in his keeping. Consequences: After the closing, he stays on to settle the college's financial and psychic affairs.

A freestanding set for the dance Minutiae: paint, newspaper, found objects, and fabric on an open wooden structure, recalling a Japanese screen. Cunningham: colors and comic strips everywhere; you could pass through it, under it, around it; made of things picked up in the street. It grew out of Albers's studies of matière and color and Anni Albers's weavings. The 1954/1976 version: 84.5 × 81 × 30.5 inches, oil, paper, fabric, newspaper, wood, metal, plastic, mirror, string Consequences: Begins the ten-year collaboration with the company and Rauschenberg's sculptural practice; one of the first Combines

Rauschenberg makes Minutiae, at once painting, sculpture, stage unit, and theatrical screen; the version exists as 1954/1976. It was a present for Cunningham, containing a private joke for the dancers. Oil, paper, fabric, newspaper, wood, metal, plastic, mirror, and string on a wooden structure, about 84 x 81 x 30 inches. Behind the outer panel where the dancers paused, strips of Otto Soglow's comic strip The Little King at eye level: “his majesty attending an exhibition of modern sculpture”. Consequences: According to the author, the sum of everything Rauschenberg learned at Black Mountain and the starting point of the postmodern era.

In the fall of 1954, Karnes and Weinrib leave the college to join Richards, Tudor, and Cage at the Gate Hill Cooperative in Stony Point, New York. This exodus, along with that of many other teachers, leaves the pot shop without anyone in charge. Consequences: A sign of the college's decline; the pot shop remains in use by students until the closing
Four couples from Black Mountain found an experimental artists' community at Stony Point. Consequences: Richards's commitment to community life, begun at BMC, continues all her life
